content:
Facts: In an intestate succession, the grandchildren of the deceased (heirs by representation) sued the surviving daughter and her family company seeking reconstruction of the estate, restitution of sums allegedly misappropriated through joint bank accounts and business dealings, nullity of a monetary donation, inclusion of business value and unpaid rents, and division of the inheritance.
Legal framework
Articles 533, 737, 782–783, 979, 2555 ICC on inheritance petition, collation, form of donations, extinction of usufruct, and notion of business; Articles 115, 167, 183(6) CPC on burden of proof, non-contestation, and assertive preclusions; principles on joint bank accounts, undue payment, simulation, and inheritance division.
Interpretative issue
Whether heirs may validly seek reduction and collation without specific pleading; how funds in joint accounts must be attributed between co-holders; whether withdrawals and transfers to a family company constitute undue payments; whether a monetary transfer qualifies as a null donation for lack of form; whether free use of property or business management gives rise to collation or restitution; and the effects of late defences and generic objections.
Principle applied
An action for reduction is inadmissible if the claimant fails to specifically allege the value of the estate, the reserved share, and the prejudicial acts. In joint bank accounts, balances are presumed to belong equally to co-holders unless timely and specific proof to the contrary is provided; unproven and generically justified withdrawals are recoverable as undue payments. Monetary donations not executed by public deed and not of modest value are null and the sums must be returned to the estate. Free use of property under a loan for use does not constitute a donation subject to collation, whereas unjustified appropriation of business assets and unpaid rents give rise to restitution claims. Assertive preclusions bar late or generic defences, and the estate must be reconstructed solely on timely pleaded facts before proceeding to division according to statutory shares. ID: ITI087; Instance_Type: First instance; Legal_Duration: P5Y8M; Law: IT – Civil Code – 737, 724, 782, 783, 1422, 533, 2555, 979; IT – Code of Civil Procedure – 115, 167, 91; State: IT; Type: Succession; Costs: Heir 2, Third party - 13.430,00; Movable_Assets: Bank account (4.308,94), Financial assets (N/A), Money/Credit (46.839,00), Money/Credit (20.000,00), Money/Credit (10.865,00), Money/Credit (16.666,66), Money/Credit (37.500,00), Money/Credit (21.950,00), Business assets (2.007,75), Money/Credit (8.107,59), Money/Credit (85.950,00); Type_of_succession: Legal succession; Second part of full text: Subsequently, on 20 January 2011, Ms THE DECEASED closed her current account in order to open another one, jointly held with the defendant, into which the balance of the previous current account was transferred. However, the joint account was also funded solely by the deceased's pension or by sums from the divestment of the deceased's securities. In particular, in February 2011, Ms HEIR 3 divested securities amounting to €14,058.85. The sum remained in the account for some time until, in December 2011, the defendant transferred the sum of €10,865.00 to the current account held in her and her husband's name, thereby taking possession of it.
In 2013, the defendant decided to change banks. In 2014, when the deceased was 92 years old, the defendant divested other mutual funds belonging to her mother; on 9 June 2014, she personally signed two bank cheques, each for the amount of €16,666.66, one made out to THIRD PARTY 3 and the other to THIRD PARTY 4, which the defendant used to purchase land zoned for building registered in the name of the company THIRD PARTY 1: the defendant therefore drew on her mother's current account to obtain the money she needed to complete the purchase; furthermore, also in 2014, on 23/09, the defendant withdrew the sum of €75,000.00 from the joint account with her mother by means of a cashier's cheque made out to THIRD PARTY 1. Other sums were withdrawn in 2015, in particular a cheque for €6,000.00 made out to THIRD PARTY 1 and €35,900.00 made out to THIRD PARTY 5. Another sum was withdrawn in November 2015, a bank cheque for €2,000.00 made out to THIRD PARTY 6. The deceased died on 30 November 2015. Before her death, the defendant withdrew the sum of €227,936.00.
Subsequently, after her mother's death, the defendant took possession of the additional the sum of €10,194.35, corresponding to half of the joint securities account held with the mother, and the additional amount of €3,173.16, equal to half of the cash balance of the current account.
All this by virtue of the formal joint ownership of the bank accounts in question. All the above-mentioned sums would have to be returned to the estate, as they belonged to the deceased and were unduly withdrawn by the defendant without the knowledge of the other heirs, or were the subject of a donation, null and void, by Ms THE DECEASED, even if given to the THIRD PARTY 1 company, given the substantial identity between the defendant and the aforementioned company. In particular, the donation of €20,000.00 would be null and void due to a defect in form, or rather, the sum would in any case be returned as a credit of the deceased. Therefore, the plaintiffs requested that the defendant be ordered to return the sums in question to the estate, and that, through the action for reduction, the estate be reconstructed for the establishment of the legal shares, after the defendants had been ordered to return the amounts due, with subsequent division.
The plaintiffs claimed that, during her lifetime, the deceased was also the owner of an 11/18 share of the usufruct of a property intended for use as a hotel, called Hotel HEIR 3, located in San Mauro Mare. The hotel had been built during her lifetime by Mr RELATIVE 1, the husband of the deceased. In 1988, Mrs THE DECEASED transferred the bare ownership of the share to her daughter, while in 2002, the plaintiffs, heirs of SPOUSE OF HEIR 3, transferred their shares to the company THIRD PARTY 1. In February 2005, a lease agreement was signed with the company THIRD PARTY 1 for a renewable period of one year, relating to the hotel property. Throughout this period, however, the defendant allegedly exploited the Hotel HEIR 3 hotel business, including through her family company THIRD PARTY 1, without paying anything to her mother, so that the value of the business, corresponding to the deceased's share of the property, should be included in the estate's assets. Furthermore, the plaintiffs claimed that the deceased never received the rent for the property provided for in the two contracts; this circumstance - in addition to the low rent - constituted proof that the lease agreement was, in fact, simulated, concealing a loan for use agreement and therefore an indirect donation subject to collation, corresponding to the rental value of the property calculated at the time of the opening of the succession and for all the years of the lease; the plaintiffs expressed their intention to proceed with an action for reduction of direct and indirect donations, subject to assessment by a court-appointed expert of the rent, estimated at €35,000.00 per annum, to be attributed to the defendant's share of the inheritance. In the alternative, in the plaintiffs' opinion, the lease agreement should be considered a mixed transaction with donation for having created a very low rent to the detriment of the interests of the deceased.
The defendants did not appear in court in a timely manner with a statement of defence and response, concluding with the rejection of the plaintiff's claims and the award of legal costs.
The defendants objected that, contrary to the plaintiffs' claims, the joint bank account held by the defendant and the deceased had been funded not only with money belonging to the deceased, but also with payments made by the defendant and her husband, amounting to thousands of euros. Therefore, the plaintiffs' claims were unfounded. The funds referred to by the plaintiffs on page 5 of the writ of summons had been released to pay the expenses of the HEIR 3 hotel, which had accrued in the meantime, while the sum of €20,000.00 had been donated by Ms THE DECEASED to the company THIRD PARTY 1 out of generosity and gratitude; furthermore, the said company has only had Ms HEIR 3 as a general partner since the end of 2013. With regard to the closure of account 0007168 and the transfer of the related funds to a joint account, the defendants pointed out that this new account had, from the outset, a deposit by the defendant of €200.00. The amount of €77,704.00 was also used to pay hotel expenses. They also disputed that the decision to change banks was attributable to the defendant's initiative, emphasising that it was instead taken by Ms THE DECEASED herself. All other sums claimed by the plaintiffs were expenses related to the management of Hotel HEIR 3; furthermore, in 2014/2015, the defendant also made payments. Following the death, in accordance with the bank's instructions, the sum of €2,154.47 was transferred to the defendant together with 50% of the securities. The remainder was transferred to a joint account held by the heirs, while the funeral expenses are still pending. The banking transactions carried out during Ms THE DECEASED's lifetime were also carried out on Ms THE DECEASED's initiative in accordance with her needs, especially in recent times, and also to repay sums that had been advanced by third parties, such as those for the nursing home.
The defendants then objected to the validity of the claim, arguing that it was entirely generic and inadmissible, and that it was unfounded, particularly with regard to issues relating to Hotel HEIR 3, which, following various transfers, was owned by the company THIRD PARTY 1, as there was no evidence of the existence of a business. They argued that the conditions for granting the plaintiff's claims did not exist.
The case was investigated on the basis of documentary evidence, two court-appointed expert reports and oral evidence.
The case essentially concerns the reconstruction of the estate of Mrs THE DECEASED, with the addition to the estate assets of sums allegedly belonging to the estate but subject to alleged 'appropriation', in various forms, by the defendant, and the division according to the legal shares of the estate thus reconstructed.
It is not disputed between the parties that Ms THE DECEASED, mother of the defendant and grandmother of the plaintiffs, died on 30 November 2015 without leaving a will, so that the succession was opened intestate. The status and identity of the heirs are not disputed, namely HEIR 3, heir to 50% of the estate, and the plaintiffs, representing their predeceased mother, each to 25% of the estate (see doc. 2 plaintiff's file, p. 10 court-appointed expert report filed on 27 August 2020).
As we have seen, the composition of the estate is disputed, which, in the plaintiffs' opinion, should be replenished with sums allegedly owed by the defendant for various reasons.
As a preliminary point and in law, it is worth noting that the plaintiffs, inter alia, propose to bring an action for reduction. However, this claim is clearly inadmissible, since the plaintiffs have failed to indicate the exact amount of the estate, the reserved portion, or the extent to which the portion reserved for the plaintiffs themselves has been infringed, so that the burden of proof incumbent upon them has not been satisfied (see cf. Civil Cassation, Section 2, Judgment No. 20830 of 14/10/2016; Section 2, Judgment No. 13310 of 12/09/2002). There is also no clear indication by the plaintiffs as to the precise dispositive act (donation, in the absence of a will) that is detrimental to the legitimate portion and to what extent it should be reduced, rendering the claim irremediably generic and inadmissible.
As for the rest, the plaintiffs allege that the defendant appropriated sums belonging to the deceased, which, according to the plaintiffs, were taken by the defendant without authorisation or justification. They also allege the existence of gifts subject to collation and the simulation of a lease agreement (doc. 36, plaintiff's file), which, in their opinion, conceals a loan for use or a mixed contract with a gift. It is worth noting, however, that even if the claim of simulation of the contract were upheld, no sum could in any case be attributed to the assets of the estate, since the enjoyment of a property granted free of charge by the deceased does not constitute a donation subject to collation; in particular: 'In matters of inheritance division, the free use of a property granted during the lifetime of the deceased to one of the heirs, which must necessarily be classified as a loan for use contract, cannot be qualified as a donation subject to collation, given that the benefit for the borrower consists in the personal, free and temporary use of the property, the obligation of restitution being inherent in the causal scheme of the contract. These peculiarities are incompatible with the unlimited renunciation of the availability of the asset that characterises the structure and purpose of the donation, in which the aforementioned benefit constitutes the final result of the act carried out by the parties' (Civil Court, Section 2 - Judgment No. 27259 of 16/11/2017); thus, the plaintiffs appear to have no interest in the claim of simulation, given the above premises.
As for the rest, the plaintiffs request the 'collation' of all donations, direct or indirect, as well as the transfer of the funds allegedly withdrawn by the defendant.
With regard to the first point, case law has highlighted that "The prerequisite for the obligation of collation, pursuant to Article 737 of the Italian Civil Code, is that the person subject to it has received assets or rights by way of a gift from the deceased, either directly or indirectly through payments made by the latter" (Civil Court, Section 6 - 2, Order No. 1506 of 22/01/2018). In particular, 'In the case of donations made during the lifetime of the deceased, the collation of the estate - in both forms provided for by law, by transfer of the asset in kind or by imputation - is a legal instrument aimed at forming the estate to be divided in order to ensure balance and equal treatment among the various co-heirs, so as not to alter the value ratio between the various shares, to be determined in relation to the extent of each co-heir's right, on the basis of the sum of the 'relictum' and the 'donatum' at the time of the opening of the succession, and thus guaranteeing each of the heirs the possibility of obtaining a quantity of assets proportionate to their share. It follows that the obligation of collation arises automatically following the opening of the succession' (Civil Cassation, Section 2, Judgment No. 15131 of 18/07/2005 (Rv. 582041 - 01); the persons required to make the collation are the children and their descendants and the spouse who are entitled to the succession (Article 737 of the Italian Civil Code).
Instead, according to some, the claim for recovery and allocation to the estate of the sums allegedly embezzled by the defendant is in the nature of a petition for inheritance (Article 533 of the Italian Civil Code), which '...is an action for conviction with a necessarily recuperative content, in that it is aimed at obtaining, subject to verification of the status of heir, the return of all or part of the inherited assets from anyone who possesses them without title or as an heir" (Court of Piacenza, 02/05/2018, (hearing 30/04/2018, filed 02/05/2018), no. 335; DeJure); recent case law, on the other hand, is contrary to this approach, noting that '...the claim for restitution of the sums that the defendant allegedly withdrew from the deceased's account, as joint account holder, ... does not fall within the scope of Article 22 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure as a 'petition'. With a petition, in fact, 'the heir can only claim the assets to which he or she is entitled mortis causa from the deceased, i.e. the assets that were included in the estate at the time of the opening of the succession; it follows that such an action cannot be brought to include in the succession sums of money that the deceased, prior to his death, remitted by means of bank cheques, without any apparent justification, to the future heir and that the latter has or had at his disposal by virtue of a pre-existing legal title independent of the death of the deceased" (Cass. No. 3181/2011)" (Cass. Civ. Sez. 6 - 2, Order No. 11879 of 12/04/2022), taking into account the different configuration of the action as a claim for the recovery of an objective undue payment (cf. Court of Taranto, 09/02/2022, No. 328; DeJure), as payments without justification (cf. Cass. Civ. Sez. 2 - , Judgment no. 30713 of 27/11/2018).
Having clarified this, it is necessary to proceed with the reconstruction of the estate of Mrs THE DECEASED. On this point, it should first be emphasised and stated that any determination must be made only with reference to the claims and allegations made in a timely manner by the plaintiffs in compliance with the limitation periods; any further circumstances, even if represented and ascertained during the expert's investigations, but not promptly submitted by the parties, shall therefore be irrelevant; as is well known, in fact, '...the preclusion regime is intended not only to protect the interests of the parties, but also the public interest in avoiding prolonging the proceedings, so that the such non-compliance must be noted ex officio by the judge, regardless of the procedural attitude of the other party" (Civil Court, Section 2 - Judgment No. 17121 of 13/08/2020); it should also be noted that defendants who appear late in court are precluded from raising counterclaims or exceptions that cannot be detected ex officio.
The first asset of the estate is certainly composed, given that the data is not disputed, of 50% of the credit balance of ordinary current account no. CC0190136696 at Cassa di Risparmio di Ravenna, jointly held with the defendant, bearing the amount of €4,308.94 at the date of death (see documents 44, 45 in the plaintiff's file, page 17 of the court-appointed expert's report filed on 27 August 2020). In the plaintiffs' opinion, the money in the account, although jointly held with the defendant, should be attributed in full to Ms THE DECEASED. On the other hand, in the opinion of the defendants, Ms HEIR 3 contributed to the balance of the current account by making deposits of at least €29,000.00, while the defendant's husband made additional deposits of thousands of euros (page 3 of the statement of defence and reply): as noted by the defendants in the second brief pursuant to Article 183(6) of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure, this circumstance was not promptly and precisely contested by the plaintiffs either at the hearing or in the first brief pursuant to Article 183(6) of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure, the deadline for assertive preclusions. Article 115 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure requires that 'the judge must base his decision on the evidence presented by the parties or by the public prosecutor, as well as on the facts not specifically contested by the defendant', so that the attached payments must be considered proven, as the plaintiff failed to contest the historical fact alleged by the other party in a precise and timely manner. As is well known, in the case of a joint current account, the parties are presumed to be equal, unless otherwise proven (see Civil Court, Section 3, Judgment No. 4496 of 24/02/2010). In the present case, as we have seen, it must be considered proven that the current account in question was also fed by payments from the defendant, and therefore it appears correct to attribute to the estate only 50% of the credit balance of the current account in question at the date of death (1).
In the plaintiff's narrative, it is stated that at the time of death, the deceased was also the holder of a securities account jointly held with her daughter HEIR 3 (plaintiff's document 3), which, in the plaintiffs' opinion, consisted of securities belonging solely to Ms THE DECEASED, transferred from a previous deposit held solely in the name of THE DECEASED and closed on 24 April 2006 (doc. 10 plaintiff's file). At the date of death, this securities account had a value of €20,388.71.
The plaintiff's claim does not appear to have been effectively and promptly contested.
Therefore, 100% of the securities held in the administered deposit on the date of death must be attributed to the assets of the estate (2).
The plaintiffs also allege that the defendant misappropriated numerous sums belonging to their mother.
The first would be the sum of €46,839.00, transferred from the current account in the name of the mother on 25 January 2008 to that of the defendant (doc. 14 plaintiff's file, transfer signed by HEIR 3); the defendants claim that the sum was used to pay the expenses incurred in the meantime by the HEIR 3 hotel (a building used as a summer hotel located in San Mauro Pascoli, see doc. 35 bis plaintiff's file), of which the deceased was the usufructuary for the 11/18 share, having donated the bare ownership to the defendant and the plaintiffs, in their respective shares of 1⁄2, 1⁄4 and 1⁄4 (see doc. 35 bis, cit., p. 3); However, the statement appears to be entirely generic and unspecified in terms of the expiry of the assertive preclusions, as it does not indicate precisely what expenses are involved, their nature, amount, etc., and the indistinct production of the documents and invoices referred to in doc. 3 and doc. 4 produced by the defendants together with the second brief pursuant to Article 183(6) of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure, in the absence of precise and timely defensive allegations; it is well known, as emphasised by case law, that 'the defendant, in response to a clear and detailed factual allegation by the plaintiff, has the burden under Article 167 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure to take an analytical position on the circumstances whose veracity it intends to contest...' (Civil Cassation, Section 6 - 3, Order No. 9439 of 23/03/2022): therefore, the amount of €46,839.00 must be counted as an asset of the estate, as it was unduly withdrawn and must therefore be returned to the estate (3).
With regard to the sum of €20,000.00, it should be noted that the cheque (doc. 15 in the plaintiff's file, dated 25 January 2008) is signed by THE DECEASED and made payable to THIRD PARTY 1 and therefore there is no basis for attributing it to the estate either as a donation subject to collation, as THIRD PARTY 1 is not subject to collation, nor as unjust enrichment to the benefit of the defendant, as it is the result of a dispositive act by the deceased addressed to a legal entity that is completely independent and distinct from the co-heir. The plaintiffs, however, allege that this disposition of assets would in any case constitute a null and void donation due to a defect of form: the donative nature of the asset allocation in question, granted by THE DECEASED 'in a spirit of generosity and gratitude' (page 3 of the statement of defence) is admitted by the defendants themselves. As is well known, donations must be made by public deed, under penalty of nullity (Article 782 of the Italian Civil Code), with the exception of donations of modest value (Article 783 of the Italian Civil Code). In case law, it is pointed out that 'Donations of modest value (Article 783 of the Civil Code), for which no written form is required 'substantiam', must be assessed on the basis of two criteria: the objective criterion, related to the value of the asset in question, and the subjective criterion, which takes into account the economic conditions of the donor. It follows that, in order to be considered of modest value, the act of generosity must never have an appreciable impact on the donor's assets" (Civil Cassation, Section 1, Judgment No. 11304 of 30/12/1994 (Rv. 489470 - 01): in the case in question, it is clear that the donation of €20,000.00 cannot be considered 'of modest value', especially considering the economic conditions of the donor, whose movable assets, as far as is known, amounted to around €300,000 at the time (see documents 8 and 12 in the plaintiff's file). The nullity of the donation, insofar as it lacks formal validity, means that the donee (THIRD PARTY 1) is required to return the donated sum to the estate (see Civil Court, Section 1 - Order No. 5488 of 18/02/2022): the assets therefore also include the sum of €20,000.00 (4).
According to the plaintiffs, during 2011, the defendant unlawfully took possession of the sum of €10,865.00 (document 20 in the plaintiff's file) by transferring the sum to an account in the defendant's name. According to the defendants, these were hotel expenses to be paid, and they allege (first statement pursuant to Article 183(6) of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure) that, in any case, there is no proof of the identity of the person who made the transfer. However, the defendants' objection is generic and contradictory, and unproven, as the defendants have not fulfilled their obligation to take a specific position on the fact alleged by the plaintiffs, as already mentioned above; the account of origin (no. 1965529), as agreed between the parties and documented (doc. 20 cited), is jointly held by HEIR 3 and THE DECEASED, and in this regard, the defendants allege a documented payment, albeit of a very modest amount (€200.00), so that the plaintiffs' assertion (page 6, second paragraph of the writ of summons) that the sums that fed into this account were essentially attributable to the plaintiff (see doc. 20 cited) does not appear to be effectively refuted, either by allegation or by evidence: therefore, the amount of €10,865.00 must be attributed to the estate's assets (5).
In the plaintiffs' opinion, two cheques signed by HEIR 3, each for the amount of €16,666.66 (docs. 25 and 26 in the plaintiff's file), should also be included, which the defendant allegedly used to purchase land registered in the name of the THIRD PARTY 1 company, misappropriating her mother's money for the benefit of the family business. It should be noted that the cheques are debited from the joint account No. 136696, which, for the reasons stated above, is attributable to the deceased only for 50%. Therefore, any amounts subject to collation/allocation to the estate may amount to a maximum of €8,333.33. In the defendants' opinion, these amounts are sums paid in reimbursement of expenses advanced by the defendant. The defendants' defence appears to be generic and unproven, so that the total amount of €16,666.66 (8,333.33 x 2) must be attributed to the estate (6).
The plaintiffs alleged that the defendant also appropriated the amount of €75,000.00 through a cashier's cheque made out to THIRD PARTY 1 (doc. 28 plaintiff's file), support current account no. 136696 (doc. 29 plaintiff's file): the defendants claim that the documents do not certify the disposing party and that, in any case, the sums relate to necessary and due expenses; on this point, the considerations made above regarding the generality of the dispute apply; given the support account, the sum to be attributed to the estate amounts to €37,500.00 (7).
Finally, the plaintiffs attached further withdrawals for the amount of €6,000.00 in August 2015, €35,900.00 in September 2015 by cheque and a withdrawal of €2,000.00 by cheque (docs. 31, 32, 33); the cheques are signed by HEIR 3 and the debit account is no. 136696. The amounts are to be attributed to the estate at a rate of 50%, for all the reasons already stated above (including the generality of the defendants' arguments), for a total of €21,950.00 (8).
The sums subsequent to death have already been dealt with above.
Finally, the plaintiffs allege that the defendant took possession of the "business" known as Hotel HEIR 3, leasing it through the company THIRD PARTY 1 starting in 2005. It should be noted, however, that a clear distinction must be made between the property, which is the subject of the lease agreements and the donation of bare ownership by the deceased (see documents 35 bis, 36, 39), and the business, which consists of the complex of assets organised by the entrepreneur for the operation of the business (Article 2555 of the Italian Civil Code).
With regard to the property located in San Mauro Mare, the deceased had, as we have seen, donated the bare ownership of 11/18 of the property registered in her name to her daughter and grandchildren, reserving the usufruct for herself. As highlighted by case law, usufruct is not transferable 'mortis causa' as it expires upon the death of the owner pursuant to Article 979 of the Italian Civil Code (see Civil Court, Section 2, Judgment No. 20788 of 14/10/2015). lastly, it should be noted that the plaintiffs do not seem to clearly invoke the collation by the defendant of the bare ownership of the 11/18 share of the property; in any case, this seems to be excluded, since, from reading the deed of donation in document 35 bis of the plaintiff, it would appear that the transfer free of charge took place not only in favour of the defendant, but also of the plaintiffs, pro rata in the ratio of 2/4 to HEIR 3, 1⁄4 to HEIR 1, 1⁄4 to HEIR 2 and therefore in accordance with the inheritance shares (see page 36 of the court-appointed expert's report filed on 27 August 2020).
As regards the company, its very existence is disputed between the parties (see also page 36 of the court-appointed expert's report filed on 27 August 2020): the defendants claim, in particular, that even if the deceased may have managed or rented the company at the time (see doc. 37 in the plaintiff's file), said company had not been operational for a long time, as the THIRD PARTY 1 company had rebuilt the company from scratch (see page 4 of the defendants' second brief pursuant to Article 183(6) of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure). According to the plaintiffs, however, the business was unlawfully 'transferred' from the deceased to the defendant in 2005, who then managed it for her own benefit in subsequent transactions.
On this point, the court-appointed expert commented at length in the report filed in the case records on 27 August 2020, which, proceeding with a comparative analysis of the documentation produced in the case records by the parties (see the court-appointed expert's report, pp. 40, 41, 42, 43), highlighted the existence of numerous omissions and inconsistencies and noted that 'The opinion of the writer ... is that, in fact, until 1998, the company existed ... was owned by THE DECEASED, HEIR 1 and SPOUSE OF HEIR 3....evidently, some change occurred afterwards because in 2005 – without any transfer of ownership – the same company was leased (as grantor) by THIRD PARTY 1 s.a.s.. It must therefore be assumed that, in reality, in the absence of other supporting documents, there has been a sort of "dispossession" by THIRD PARTY 1... in the documents produced by the parties, there is no trace of the "legitimate titles" on the basis of which THIRD PARTY 1 s.a.s. has the use of this company. There is no deed of purchase, donation, loan or rental agreement, or anything else. In the opinion of the writer, therefore, it has not been proven that THIRD PARTY 1 s.a.s. has 'legitimate ownership' of the company called 'Hotel HEIR 3', which must still be considered the property and in the possession of THE DECEASED – obviously on a pro rata basis – and the other co-owners with legitimate title... Consequently, the undersigned believes that the estate of THE DECEASED is entitled to compensation for having been dispossessed of the (sole) movable and intangible part of the company called Hotel HEIR 3 (pages 43, 44 of the court-appointed expert's report filed on 27 August 2020)... another problematic aspect is the identification of the share of the company owned by THE DECEASED": on this point, the court-appointed expert agrees with the argument that, at the date of death, the company should be considered essentially owned by the defendant and the deceased, in presumably equal shares; moreover, in the absence of further evidence and in the absence of certain proof of what the plaintiffs assert – namely that the share at the date of death was 11/18, like the property – it seems possible to agree with the argument that the shares should be presumed to be equal, as noted by the court-appointed expert where he observes that 'in the opinion of the writer, the shares must be presumed to be equal, as the reliance on what was indicated (incorrectly, moreover) by THE DECEASED in her tax return, as well as the implied assumption that the shares of ownership of the company must be equal to the corresponding shares of the building (usufruct in relation to THE DECEASED) is not corroborated by any documentary evidence or logical connection (the ownership of a company that also includes a property does not necessarily coincide with the ownership of that property). Ultimately, in the opinion of this court-appointed expert, at the date of the opening of THE DECEASED's succession, the estate must include claims against THIRD PARTY 1 s.a.s., the user of the 'Hotel HEIR 3' business, for the following reasons:
•        Annual compensation from 2005 to 2019 for the operation (through additional rent) of the 'Hotel HEIR 3' business, limited to the movable property and goodwill ..., as the real estate portion is already covered by rent (i);
•        Value of the company on the date of commencement of succession, again limited to the movable part of the goodwill, since the immovable part – held by THE DECEASED in usufruct – was reunited with the bare ownership (formerly of THIRD PARTY 1 sas) as a result of the death of the usufructuary (ii).
The court-appointed expert then goes on to indicate and justify the parameters and criteria used to estimate the above elements, from which derives (ii) the value of the company on the date of the opening of the succession, limited to the 1⁄2 share of Ms THE DECEASED and only to movable property and goodwill, amounting to a total of €2,007.75 (9) (page 55 of the court-appointed expert's report filed on 27 August 2020). The court-appointed expert continues his discussion on the assessment of the amount of the rent (i), in its various components, since, as mentioned above, this compensation is due only for the non-real estate portion of the business (page 53 of the court-appointed expert's report). The amount due as rent is €8,107.59 (10), already referring to the 50% share, calculated, however, on the basis of the scheme referred to on page 55 of the court-appointed expert's report, on the date of the subsequent opening, as the subsequent items (up to 2019 and therefore after death) appear to be unrelated to the present judgment.
Finally, the plaintiffs argue that the rent for the property referred to in documents 36 and 39 was never received by Ms THE DECEASED, so that the value corresponding to the rent for the period 2005-2015 should be attributed to the defendant's share of the inheritance. T; law: Divorce

Subsequently, on 20 January 2011, Ms THE DECEASED closed her current account in order to open another one, jointly held with the defendant, into which the balance of the previous current account was transferred. However, the joint account was also funded solely by the deceased's pension or by sums from the divestment of the deceased's securities. In particular, in February 2011, Ms HEIR 3 divested securities amounting to €14,058.85. The sum remained in the account for some time until, in December 2011, the defendant transferred the sum of €10,865.00 to the current account held in her and her husband's name, thereby taking possession of it.
In 2013, the defendant decided to change banks. In 2014, when the deceased was 92 years old, the defendant divested other mutual funds belonging to her mother; on 9 June 2014, she personally signed two bank cheques, each for the amount of €16,666.66, one made out to THIRD PARTY 3 and the other to THIRD PARTY 4, which the defendant used to purchase land zoned for building registered in the name of the company THIRD PARTY 1: the defendant therefore drew on her mother's current account to obtain the money she needed to complete the purchase; furthermore, also in 2014, on 23/09, the defendant withdrew the sum of €75,000.00 from the joint account with her mother by means of a cashier's cheque made out to THIRD PARTY 1. Other sums were withdrawn in 2015, in particular a cheque for €6,000.00 made out to THIRD PARTY 1 and €35,900.00 made out to THIRD PARTY 5. Another sum was withdrawn in November 2015, a bank cheque for €2,000.00 made out to THIRD PARTY 6. The deceased died on 30 November 2015. Before her death, the defendant withdrew the sum of €227,936.00.
Subsequently, after her mother's death, the defendant took possession of the additional the sum of €10,194.35, corresponding to half of the joint securities account held with the mother, and the additional amount of €3,173.16, equal to half of the cash balance of the current account.
All this by virtue of the formal joint ownership of the bank accounts in question. All the above-mentioned sums would have to be returned to the estate, as they belonged to the deceased and were unduly withdrawn by the defendant without the knowledge of the other heirs, or were the subject of a donation, null and void, by Ms THE DECEASED, even if given to the THIRD PARTY 1 company, given the substantial identity between the defendant and the aforementioned company. In particular, the donation of €20,000.00 would be null and void due to a defect in form, or rather, the sum would in any case be returned as a credit of the deceased. Therefore, the plaintiffs requested that the defendant be ordered to return the sums in question to the estate, and that, through the action for reduction, the estate be reconstructed for the establishment of the legal shares, after the defendants had been ordered to return the amounts due, with subsequent division.
The plaintiffs claimed that, during her lifetime, the deceased was also the owner of an 11/18 share of the usufruct of a property intended for use as a hotel, called Hotel HEIR 3, located in San Mauro Mare. The hotel had been built during her lifetime by Mr RELATIVE 1, the husband of the deceased. In 1988, Mrs THE DECEASED transferred the bare ownership of the share to her daughter, while in 2002, the plaintiffs, heirs of SPOUSE OF HEIR 3, transferred their shares to the company THIRD PARTY 1. In February 2005, a lease agreement was signed with the company THIRD PARTY 1 for a renewable period of one year, relating to the hotel property. Throughout this period, however, the defendant allegedly exploited the Hotel HEIR 3 hotel business, including through her family company THIRD PARTY 1, without paying anything to her mother, so that the value of the business, corresponding to the deceased's share of the property, should be included in the estate's assets. Furthermore, the plaintiffs claimed that the deceased never received the rent for the property provided for in the two contracts; this circumstance - in addition to the low rent - constituted proof that the lease agreement was, in fact, simulated, concealing a loan for use agreement and therefore an indirect donation subject to collation, corresponding to the rental value of the property calculated at the time of the opening of the succession and for all the years of the lease; the plaintiffs expressed their intention to proceed with an action for reduction of direct and indirect donations, subject to assessment by a court-appointed expert of the rent, estimated at €35,000.00 per annum, to be attributed to the defendant's share of the inheritance. In the alternative, in the plaintiffs' opinion, the lease agreement should be considered a mixed transaction with donation for having created a very low rent to the detriment of the interests of the deceased.
The defendants did not appear in court in a timely manner with a statement of defence and response, concluding with the rejection of the plaintiff's claims and the award of legal costs.
The defendants objected that, contrary to the plaintiffs' claims, the joint bank account held by the defendant and the deceased had been funded not only with money belonging to the deceased, but also with payments made by the defendant and her husband, amounting to thousands of euros. Therefore, the plaintiffs' claims were unfounded. The funds referred to by the plaintiffs on page 5 of the writ of summons had been released to pay the expenses of the HEIR 3 hotel, which had accrued in the meantime, while the sum of €20,000.00 had been donated by Ms THE DECEASED to the company THIRD PARTY 1 out of generosity and gratitude; furthermore, the said company has only had Ms HEIR 3 as a general partner since the end of 2013. With regard to the closure of account 0007168 and the transfer of the related funds to a joint account, the defendants pointed out that this new account had, from the outset, a deposit by the defendant of €200.00. The amount of €77,704.00 was also used to pay hotel expenses. They also disputed that the decision to change banks was attributable to the defendant's initiative, emphasising that it was instead taken by Ms THE DECEASED herself. All other sums claimed by the plaintiffs were expenses related to the management of Hotel HEIR 3; furthermore, in 2014/2015, the defendant also made payments. Following the death, in accordance with the bank's instructions, the sum of €2,154.47 was transferred to the defendant together with 50% of the securities. The remainder was transferred to a joint account held by the heirs, while the funeral expenses are still pending. The banking transactions carried out during Ms THE DECEASED's lifetime were also carried out on Ms THE DECEASED's initiative in accordance with her needs, especially in recent times, and also to repay sums that had been advanced by third parties, such as those for the nursing home.
The defendants then objected to the validity of the claim, arguing that it was entirely generic and inadmissible, and that it was unfounded, particularly with regard to issues relating to Hotel HEIR 3, which, following various transfers, was owned by the company THIRD PARTY 1, as there was no evidence of the existence of a business. They argued that the conditions for granting the plaintiff's claims did not exist.
The case was investigated on the basis of documentary evidence, two court-appointed expert reports and oral evidence.
The case essentially concerns the reconstruction of the estate of Mrs THE DECEASED, with the addition to the estate assets of sums allegedly belonging to the estate but subject to alleged 'appropriation', in various forms, by the defendant, and the division according to the legal shares of the estate thus reconstructed.
It is not disputed between the parties that Ms THE DECEASED, mother of the defendant and grandmother of the plaintiffs, died on 30 November 2015 without leaving a will, so that the succession was opened intestate. The status and identity of the heirs are not disputed, namely HEIR 3, heir to 50% of the estate, and the plaintiffs, representing their predeceased mother, each to 25% of the estate (see doc. 2 plaintiff's file, p. 10 court-appointed expert report filed on 27 August 2020).
As we have seen, the composition of the estate is disputed, which, in the plaintiffs' opinion, should be replenished with sums allegedly owed by the defendant for various reasons.
As a preliminary point and in law, it is worth noting that the plaintiffs, inter alia, propose to bring an action for reduction. However, this claim is clearly inadmissible, since the plaintiffs have failed to indicate the exact amount of the estate, the reserved portion, or the extent to which the portion reserved for the plaintiffs themselves has been infringed, so that the burden of proof incumbent upon them has not been satisfied (see cf. Civil Cassation, Section 2, Judgment No. 20830 of 14/10/2016; Section 2, Judgment No. 13310 of 12/09/2002). There is also no clear indication by the plaintiffs as to the precise dispositive act (donation, in the absence of a will) that is detrimental to the legitimate portion and to what extent it should be reduced, rendering the claim irremediably generic and inadmissible.
As for the rest, the plaintiffs allege that the defendant appropriated sums belonging to the deceased, which, according to the plaintiffs, were taken by the defendant without authorisation or justification. They also allege the existence of gifts subject to collation and the simulation of a lease agreement (doc. 36, plaintiff's file), which, in their opinion, conceals a loan for use or a mixed contract with a gift. It is worth noting, however, that even if the claim of simulation of the contract were upheld, no sum could in any case be attributed to the assets of the estate, since the enjoyment of a property granted free of charge by the deceased does not constitute a donation subject to collation; in particular: 'In matters of inheritance division, the free use of a property granted during the lifetime of the deceased to one of the heirs, which must necessarily be classified as a loan for use contract, cannot be qualified as a donation subject to collation, given that the benefit for the borrower consists in the personal, free and temporary use of the property, the obligation of restitution being inherent in the causal scheme of the contract. These peculiarities are incompatible with the unlimited renunciation of the availability of the asset that characterises the structure and purpose of the donation, in which the aforementioned benefit constitutes the final result of the act carried out by the parties' (Civil Court, Section 2 - Judgment No. 27259 of 16/11/2017); thus, the plaintiffs appear to have no interest in the claim of simulation, given the above premises.
As for the rest, the plaintiffs request the 'collation' of all donations, direct or indirect, as well as the transfer of the funds allegedly withdrawn by the defendant.
With regard to the first point, case law has highlighted that "The prerequisite for the obligation of collation, pursuant to Article 737 of the Italian Civil Code, is that the person subject to it has received assets or rights by way of a gift from the deceased, either directly or indirectly through payments made by the latter" (Civil Court, Section 6 - 2, Order No. 1506 of 22/01/2018). In particular, 'In the case of donations made during the lifetime of the deceased, the collation of the estate - in both forms provided for by law, by transfer of the asset in kind or by imputation - is a legal instrument aimed at forming the estate to be divided in order to ensure balance and equal treatment among the various co-heirs, so as not to alter the value ratio between the various shares, to be determined in relation to the extent of each co-heir's right, on the basis of the sum of the 'relictum' and the 'donatum' at the time of the opening of the succession, and thus guaranteeing each of the heirs the possibility of obtaining a quantity of assets proportionate to their share. It follows that the obligation of collation arises automatically following the opening of the succession' (Civil Cassation, Section 2, Judgment No. 15131 of 18/07/2005 (Rv. 582041 - 01); the persons required to make the collation are the children and their descendants and the spouse who are entitled to the succession (Article 737 of the Italian Civil Code).
Instead, according to some, the claim for recovery and allocation to the estate of the sums allegedly embezzled by the defendant is in the nature of a petition for inheritance (Article 533 of the Italian Civil Code), which '...is an action for conviction with a necessarily recuperative content, in that it is aimed at obtaining, subject to verification of the status of heir, the return of all or part of the inherited assets from anyone who possesses them without title or as an heir" (Court of Piacenza, 02/05/2018, (hearing 30/04/2018, filed 02/05/2018), no. 335; DeJure); recent case law, on the other hand, is contrary to this approach, noting that '...the claim for restitution of the sums that the defendant allegedly withdrew from the deceased's account, as joint account holder, ... does not fall within the scope of Article 22 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure as a 'petition'. With a petition, in fact, 'the heir can only claim the assets to which he or she is entitled mortis causa from the deceased, i.e. the assets that were included in the estate at the time of the opening of the succession; it follows that such an action cannot be brought to include in the succession sums of money that the deceased, prior to his death, remitted by means of bank cheques, without any apparent justification, to the future heir and that the latter has or had at his disposal by virtue of a pre-existing legal title independent of the death of the deceased" (Cass. No. 3181/2011)" (Cass. Civ. Sez. 6 - 2, Order No. 11879 of 12/04/2022), taking into account the different configuration of the action as a claim for the recovery of an objective undue payment (cf. Court of Taranto, 09/02/2022, No. 328; DeJure), as payments without justification (cf. Cass. Civ. Sez. 2 - , Judgment no. 30713 of 27/11/2018).
Having clarified this, it is necessary to proceed with the reconstruction of the estate of Mrs THE DECEASED. On this point, it should first be emphasised and stated that any determination must be made only with reference to the claims and allegations made in a timely manner by the plaintiffs in compliance with the limitation periods; any further circumstances, even if represented and ascertained during the expert's investigations, but not promptly submitted by the parties, shall therefore be irrelevant; as is well known, in fact, '...the preclusion regime is intended not only to protect the interests of the parties, but also the public interest in avoiding prolonging the proceedings, so that the such non-compliance must be noted ex officio by the judge, regardless of the procedural attitude of the other party" (Civil Court, Section 2 - Judgment No. 17121 of 13/08/2020); it should also be noted that defendants who appear late in court are precluded from raising counterclaims or exceptions that cannot be detected ex officio.
The first asset of the estate is certainly composed, given that the data is not disputed, of 50% of the credit balance of ordinary current account no. CC0190136696 at Cassa di Risparmio di Ravenna, jointly held with the defendant, bearing the amount of €4,308.94 at the date of death (see documents 44, 45 in the plaintiff's file, page 17 of the court-appointed expert's report filed on 27 August 2020). In the plaintiffs' opinion, the money in the account, although jointly held with the defendant, should be attributed in full to Ms THE DECEASED. On the other hand, in the opinion of the defendants, Ms HEIR 3 contributed to the balance of the current account by making deposits of at least €29,000.00, while the defendant's husband made additional deposits of thousands of euros (page 3 of the statement of defence and reply): as noted by the defendants in the second brief pursuant to Article 183(6) of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure, this circumstance was not promptly and precisely contested by the plaintiffs either at the hearing or in the first brief pursuant to Article 183(6) of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure, the deadline for assertive preclusions. Article 115 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure requires that 'the judge must base his decision on the evidence presented by the parties or by the public prosecutor, as well as on the facts not specifically contested by the defendant', so that the attached payments must be considered proven, as the plaintiff failed to contest the historical fact alleged by the other party in a precise and timely manner. As is well known, in the case of a joint current account, the parties are presumed to be equal, unless otherwise proven (see Civil Court, Section 3, Judgment No. 4496 of 24/02/2010). In the present case, as we have seen, it must be considered proven that the current account in question was also fed by payments from the defendant, and therefore it appears correct to attribute to the estate only 50% of the credit balance of the current account in question at the date of death (1).
In the plaintiff's narrative, it is stated that at the time of death, the deceased was also the holder of a securities account jointly held with her daughter HEIR 3 (plaintiff's document 3), which, in the plaintiffs' opinion, consisted of securities belonging solely to Ms THE DECEASED, transferred from a previous deposit held solely in the name of THE DECEASED and closed on 24 April 2006 (doc. 10 plaintiff's file). At the date of death, this securities account had a value of €20,388.71.
The plaintiff's claim does not appear to have been effectively and promptly contested.
Therefore, 100% of the securities held in the administered deposit on the date of death must be attributed to the assets of the estate (2).
The plaintiffs also allege that the defendant misappropriated numerous sums belonging to their mother.
The first would be the sum of €46,839.00, transferred from the current account in the name of the mother on 25 January 2008 to that of the defendant (doc. 14 plaintiff's file, transfer signed by HEIR 3); the defendants claim that the sum was used to pay the expenses incurred in the meantime by the HEIR 3 hotel (a building used as a summer hotel located in San Mauro Pascoli, see doc. 35 bis plaintiff's file), of which the deceased was the usufructuary for the 11/18 share, having donated the bare ownership to the defendant and the plaintiffs, in their respective shares of 1⁄2, 1⁄4 and 1⁄4 (see doc. 35 bis, cit., p. 3); However, the statement appears to be entirely generic and unspecified in terms of the expiry of the assertive preclusions, as it does not indicate precisely what expenses are involved, their nature, amount, etc., and the indistinct production of the documents and invoices referred to in doc. 3 and doc. 4 produced by the defendants together with the second brief pursuant to Article 183(6) of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure, in the absence of precise and timely defensive allegations; it is well known, as emphasised by case law, that 'the defendant, in response to a clear and detailed factual allegation by the plaintiff, has the burden under Article 167 of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure to take an analytical position on the circumstances whose veracity it intends to contest...' (Civil Cassation, Section 6 - 3, Order No. 9439 of 23/03/2022): therefore, the amount of €46,839.00 must be counted as an asset of the estate, as it was unduly withdrawn and must therefore be returned to the estate (3).
With regard to the sum of €20,000.00, it should be noted that the cheque (doc. 15 in the plaintiff's file, dated 25 January 2008) is signed by THE DECEASED and made payable to THIRD PARTY 1 and therefore there is no basis for attributing it to the estate either as a donation subject to collation, as THIRD PARTY 1 is not subject to collation, nor as unjust enrichment to the benefit of the defendant, as it is the result of a dispositive act by the deceased addressed to a legal entity that is completely independent and distinct from the co-heir. The plaintiffs, however, allege that this disposition of assets would in any case constitute a null and void donation due to a defect of form: the donative nature of the asset allocation in question, granted by THE DECEASED 'in a spirit of generosity and gratitude' (page 3 of the statement of defence) is admitted by the defendants themselves. As is well known, donations must be made by public deed, under penalty of nullity (Article 782 of the Italian Civil Code), with the exception of donations of modest value (Article 783 of the Italian Civil Code). In case law, it is pointed out that 'Donations of modest value (Article 783 of the Civil Code), for which no written form is required 'substantiam', must be assessed on the basis of two criteria: the objective criterion, related to the value of the asset in question, and the subjective criterion, which takes into account the economic conditions of the donor. It follows that, in order to be considered of modest value, the act of generosity must never have an appreciable impact on the donor's assets" (Civil Cassation, Section 1, Judgment No. 11304 of 30/12/1994 (Rv. 489470 - 01): in the case in question, it is clear that the donation of €20,000.00 cannot be considered 'of modest value', especially considering the economic conditions of the donor, whose movable assets, as far as is known, amounted to around €300,000 at the time (see documents 8 and 12 in the plaintiff's file). The nullity of the donation, insofar as it lacks formal validity, means that the donee (THIRD PARTY 1) is required to return the donated sum to the estate (see Civil Court, Section 1 - Order No. 5488 of 18/02/2022): the assets therefore also include the sum of €20,000.00 (4).
According to the plaintiffs, during 2011, the defendant unlawfully took possession of the sum of €10,865.00 (document 20 in the plaintiff's file) by transferring the sum to an account in the defendant's name. According to the defendants, these were hotel expenses to be paid, and they allege (first statement pursuant to Article 183(6) of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure) that, in any case, there is no proof of the identity of the person who made the transfer. However, the defendants' objection is generic and contradictory, and unproven, as the defendants have not fulfilled their obligation to take a specific position on the fact alleged by the plaintiffs, as already mentioned above; the account of origin (no. 1965529), as agreed between the parties and documented (doc. 20 cited), is jointly held by HEIR 3 and THE DECEASED, and in this regard, the defendants allege a documented payment, albeit of a very modest amount (€200.00), so that the plaintiffs' assertion (page 6, second paragraph of the writ of summons) that the sums that fed into this account were essentially attributable to the plaintiff (see doc. 20 cited) does not appear to be effectively refuted, either by allegation or by evidence: therefore, the amount of €10,865.00 must be attributed to the estate's assets (5).
In the plaintiffs' opinion, two cheques signed by HEIR 3, each for the amount of €16,666.66 (docs. 25 and 26 in the plaintiff's file), should also be included, which the defendant allegedly used to purchase land registered in the name of the THIRD PARTY 1 company, misappropriating her mother's money for the benefit of the family business. It should be noted that the cheques are debited from the joint account No. 136696, which, for the reasons stated above, is attributable to the deceased only for 50%. Therefore, any amounts subject to collation/allocation to the estate may amount to a maximum of €8,333.33. In the defendants' opinion, these amounts are sums paid in reimbursement of expenses advanced by the defendant. The defendants' defence appears to be generic and unproven, so that the total amount of €16,666.66 (8,333.33 x 2) must be attributed to the estate (6).
The plaintiffs alleged that the defendant also appropriated the amount of €75,000.00 through a cashier's cheque made out to THIRD PARTY 1 (doc. 28 plaintiff's file), support current account no. 136696 (doc. 29 plaintiff's file): the defendants claim that the documents do not certify the disposing party and that, in any case, the sums relate to necessary and due expenses; on this point, the considerations made above regarding the generality of the dispute apply; given the support account, the sum to be attributed to the estate amounts to €37,500.00 (7).
Finally, the plaintiffs attached further withdrawals for the amount of €6,000.00 in August 2015, €35,900.00 in September 2015 by cheque and a withdrawal of €2,000.00 by cheque (docs. 31, 32, 33); the cheques are signed by HEIR 3 and the debit account is no. 136696. The amounts are to be attributed to the estate at a rate of 50%, for all the reasons already stated above (including the generality of the defendants' arguments), for a total of €21,950.00 (8).
The sums subsequent to death have already been dealt with above.
Finally, the plaintiffs allege that the defendant took possession of the "business" known as Hotel HEIR 3, leasing it through the company THIRD PARTY 1 starting in 2005. It should be noted, however, that a clear distinction must be made between the property, which is the subject of the lease agreements and the donation of bare ownership by the deceased (see documents 35 bis, 36, 39), and the business, which consists of the complex of assets organised by the entrepreneur for the operation of the business (Article 2555 of the Italian Civil Code).
With regard to the property located in San Mauro Mare, the deceased had, as we have seen, donated the bare ownership of 11/18 of the property registered in her name to her daughter and grandchildren, reserving the usufruct for herself. As highlighted by case law, usufruct is not transferable 'mortis causa' as it expires upon the death of the owner pursuant to Article 979 of the Italian Civil Code (see Civil Court, Section 2, Judgment No. 20788 of 14/10/2015). lastly, it should be noted that the plaintiffs do not seem to clearly invoke the collation by the defendant of the bare ownership of the 11/18 share of the property; in any case, this seems to be excluded, since, from reading the deed of donation in document 35 bis of the plaintiff, it would appear that the transfer free of charge took place not only in favour of the defendant, but also of the plaintiffs, pro rata in the ratio of 2/4 to HEIR 3, 1⁄4 to HEIR 1, 1⁄4 to HEIR 2 and therefore in accordance with the inheritance shares (see page 36 of the court-appointed expert's report filed on 27 August 2020).
As regards the company, its very existence is disputed between the parties (see also page 36 of the court-appointed expert's report filed on 27 August 2020): the defendants claim, in particular, that even if the deceased may have managed or rented the company at the time (see doc. 37 in the plaintiff's file), said company had not been operational for a long time, as the THIRD PARTY 1 company had rebuilt the company from scratch (see page 4 of the defendants' second brief pursuant to Article 183(6) of the Italian Code of Civil Procedure). According to the plaintiffs, however, the business was unlawfully 'transferred' from the deceased to the defendant in 2005, who then managed it for her own benefit in subsequent transactions.
On this point, the court-appointed expert commented at length in the report filed in the case records on 27 August 2020, which, proceeding with a comparative analysis of the documentation produced in the case records by the parties (see the court-appointed expert's report, pp. 40, 41, 42, 43), highlighted the existence of numerous omissions and inconsistencies and noted that 'The opinion of the writer ... is that, in fact, until 1998, the company existed ... was owned by THE DECEASED, HEIR 1 and SPOUSE OF HEIR 3....evidently, some change occurred afterwards because in 2005 – without any transfer of ownership – the same company was leased (as grantor) by THIRD PARTY 1 s.a.s.. It must therefore be assumed that, in reality, in the absence of other supporting documents, there has been a sort of "dispossession" by THIRD PARTY 1... in the documents produced by the parties, there is no trace of the "legitimate titles" on the basis of which THIRD PARTY 1 s.a.s. has the use of this company. There is no deed of purchase, donation, loan or rental agreement, or anything else. In the opinion of the writer, therefore, it has not been proven that THIRD PARTY 1 s.a.s. has 'legitimate ownership' of the company called 'Hotel HEIR 3', which must still be considered the property and in the possession of THE DECEASED – obviously on a pro rata basis – and the other co-owners with legitimate title... Consequently, the undersigned believes that the estate of THE DECEASED is entitled to compensation for having been dispossessed of the (sole) movable and intangible part of the company called Hotel HEIR 3 (pages 43, 44 of the court-appointed expert's report filed on 27 August 2020)... another problematic aspect is the identification of the share of the company owned by THE DECEASED": on this point, the court-appointed expert agrees with the argument that, at the date of death, the company should be considered essentially owned by the defendant and the deceased, in presumably equal shares; moreover, in the absence of further evidence and in the absence of certain proof of what the plaintiffs assert – namely that the share at the date of death was 11/18, like the property – it seems possible to agree with the argument that the shares should be presumed to be equal, as noted by the court-appointed expert where he observes that 'in the opinion of the writer, the shares must be presumed to be equal, as the reliance on what was indicated (incorrectly, moreover) by THE DECEASED in her tax return, as well as the implied assumption that the shares of ownership of the company must be equal to the corresponding shares of the building (usufruct in relation to THE DECEASED) is not corroborated by any documentary evidence or logical connection (the ownership of a company that also includes a property does not necessarily coincide with the ownership of that property). Ultimately, in the opinion of this court-appointed expert, at the date of the opening of THE DECEASED's succession, the estate must include claims against THIRD PARTY 1 s.a.s., the user of the 'Hotel HEIR 3' business, for the following reasons:
•        Annual compensation from 2005 to 2019 for the operation (through additional rent) of the 'Hotel HEIR 3' business, limited to the movable property and goodwill ..., as the real estate portion is already covered by rent (i);
•        Value of the company on the date of commencement of succession, again limited to the movable part of the goodwill, since the immovable part – held by THE DECEASED in usufruct – was reunited with the bare ownership (formerly of THIRD PARTY 1 sas) as a result of the death of the usufructuary (ii).
The court-appointed expert then goes on to indicate and justify the parameters and criteria used to estimate the above elements, from which derives (ii) the value of the company on the date of the opening of the succession, limited to the 1⁄2 share of Ms THE DECEASED and only to movable property and goodwill, amounting to a total of €2,007.75 (9) (page 55 of the court-appointed expert's report filed on 27 August 2020). The court-appointed expert continues his discussion on the assessment of the amount of the rent (i), in its various components, since, as mentioned above, this compensation is due only for the non-real estate portion of the business (page 53 of the court-appointed expert's report). The amount due as rent is €8,107.59 (10), already referring to the 50% share, calculated, however, on the basis of the scheme referred to on page 55 of the court-appointed expert's report, on the date of the subsequent opening, as the subsequent items (up to 2019 and therefore after death) appear to be unrelated to the present judgment.
Finally, the plaintiffs argue that the rent for the property referred to in documents 36 and 39 was never received by Ms THE DECEASED, so that the value corresponding to the rent for the period 2005-2015 should be attributed to the defendant's share of the inheritance. T
